clue.text: Is in cooler season attended by females in forest?

parts.note: female deer in a wood are does
a season is a period, a time

explanation.surface: Someone sits in a cool spot in the woods during a season with female company.
explanation.walkthrough: The season comes first in the clue but is attended by the females, who therefore stand first. 'Cooler' is slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: To serve a prison sentence is to be locked up, and cooler is informal slang for a jail.

clue.text: Release from service Old Bill shortly seen probing death

indicators.note: a probe pushes inside something, so these letters go into the middle of another word

parts.note: demise is a formal word for death

indicators.note: something put shortly is cut short, so the final letter goes

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
the name Bill, which loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Police officers are investigating a death, in the setting of someone leaving the forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Bill' reads as British slang for the police, but here the two words work separately: old is O, and Bill is a man's name trimmed by 'shortly'.
explanation.definitionFit: To demobilise is to discharge troops from active military duty once a war or campaign ends.

clue.text: Use the last supporter's ventilation equipment

parts.note: to use up the last of something is to exhaust it
a fan supports a team or star

explanation.surface: Someone is told to use the final supporter's breathing apparatus.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the possessive belongs to the supporter; it simply joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan that draws stale air or fumes out of a room is a piece of kit used for ventilation.

clue.text: Ready to drop on coming in half-drunk

indicators.note: something coming in enters, so these letters go inside another word
taking half of a word removes the rest of its letters

parts.note: tiddly is British slang for slightly drunk; only its first half is used
re means on or about, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: Someone arrives somewhat tipsy and close to collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiddly is a British word for slightly drunk, so 'half-drunk' plays on both senses; 'on' meaning concerning is a common crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone exhausted and close to collapsing from fatigue is said to be ready to drop.

clue.text: Play pubs, not clubs, in holiday island

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
'not' says this item is left out of the word

parts.note: Majorca is a Spanish Mediterranean island popular with British tourists
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
two bars, as the word is plural

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker in Majorca chooses to visit the pubs rather than the nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a verb about going round pubs; it is a noun for the definition. Removing C from MAJORCA leaves MAJORA, around two BARs.
explanation.definitionFit: Major Barbara is a stage drama by George Bernard Shaw about a Salvation Army officer.

clue.text: Get in circle: skip around by turning

parts.note: O is round like a circle

indicators.note: something placed around another surrounds it

parts.note: a skip is a large open rubbish container, so a bin

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: by and at both mean next to

explanation.surface: A children's game where you join a circle and skip round in turn.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a skip is a large builders' rubbish container, so a bin; it goes around TA after O.
explanation.definitionFit: To get in supplies is to acquire or procure them, a phrasal synonym for the answer.

clue.text: British painters fancy brooch

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are worked into a new pattern

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: British artists like the look of a piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as the verb like or desire, but it is the anagram signal after the painters.
explanation.definitionFit: A breastpin is an ornamental pin worn on the chest, which is what a brooch is.

clue.text: East after A40 for one taking wheel

indicators.note: one item placed after another follows it in the line

parts.note: A as written, then 40 in Roman numerals
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A driver heading east on the A40 road takes the steering wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: The A40 is a major British road, which suits the driving surface; here it is A plus XL, the Roman numeral for 40.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheel is mounted on the rod or shaft that runs through its centre, so that shaft takes the wheel.

clue.text: Senseless maiden wearing retro hairstyle?

indicators.note: retro means looking backwards, so the letters run in reverse
what wears something has it around it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a bun is hair coiled at the back of the head
M is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A silly young woman sports an old-fashioned hairdo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retro hairstyle' suggests a vintage look, but retro is the reversal signal; the maiden goes inside the reversed bun.
explanation.definitionFit: Numb means without feeling or sensation, which is the physical sense of senseless.

clue.text: Ruler somewhat open with a poor player making comeback

indicators.note: coming back means returning the way you came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a door ajar is partly open
taken as written
a ham is a bad, overacting performer

explanation.surface: A monarch, fairly approachable, joins a weak sportsman staging a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor player' points to sport, but a player is also an actor, and a bad one is a ham.
explanation.definitionFit: A maharaja is an Indian prince or king, the title of a sovereign over a princely state.

clue.text: Bottom to thrash in confused situation

parts.note: the bottom of a river or sea is its bed
to lam is to beat hard

explanation.surface: Someone gets a spanking amid chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom' and 'thrash' together suggest a spanking; bottom is the bed of a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam is a scene of uproar and chaos, named after a notorious London asylum.

clue.text: Mediocre work over border many a time calling in sick

indicators.note: someone calling in drops by and steps inside, so these letters go between others
in a down entry, one piece over another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: to run a machine or business is to work it
oft is an old word for often
a hem is the border of a garment
ill is a synonym for sick

explanation.surface: A lazy worker across the border keeps phoning in sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling in sick' looks like one phrase; 'calling in' puts the old word for often inside RUN-HEM, and ILL follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ordinary and unremarkable, like goods straight from a factory, is commonplace and merely average.

clue.text: Long ago one fired transport provider to stop silly mistakes

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so one piece fills the middle of another

parts.note: blunders are careless errors
a bus provides public transport

explanation.surface: A transport company sacked someone years ago to put an end to careless errors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One fired' looks like someone sacked; it is a gun, and 'long ago' marks it as an antique.
explanation.definitionFit: A blunderbuss was a short flared-muzzle musket used centuries ago, so a firearm discharged in past times.

clue.text: Loch secret out in an English town

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The secret of a Scottish lake has got out in an English town.
explanation.walkthrough: The Loch Ness monster lurks behind the surface; the town is in Essex, often called Britain's oldest recorded town.
explanation.definitionFit: Colchester is a historic market town in Essex, in the east of England.

clue.text: Mugs people in street for an amount to be paid

parts.note: mugs are gullible fools, as are asses

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street
men are people

explanation.surface: Someone robs passers-by in the street for money owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mugs' reads as the verb rob; here it is the noun, fools.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessment is a sum levied or charged, such as a tax figure or a fee fixed by valuation.

clue.text: Corrupt cartel losing capital anon

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or perverted from its proper form, so the letters are rearranged
a capital is a first letter, and losing it removes that letter from the word

parts.note: taken as written, before its first letter goes

explanation.surface: A crooked business ring will soon run out of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' suggests money, but it means the capital letter that starts the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old-fashioned word for soon or presently, meaning at a subsequent time.

clue.text: Teddy bear's associate nicely slim with tail tucked in?

indicators.note: something tucked in is pushed inside, so a letter goes into the word
the tail is the last letter, taken off the end of the word

parts.note: Roo is a friend of Winnie-the-Pooh, a bear
svelte means elegantly slender

explanation.surface: A teddy bear's companion looks pleasingly trim once its tail is tucked away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teddy bear' reads as one toy; Teddy is the definition, and the bear is Pooh. SVELTE moves its final E inside to make SEVELT.
explanation.definitionFit: Teddy was the nickname of US president Theodore Roosevelt, after whom the teddy bear was named.

clue.text: Passionate about pub — does this get rather blurry?

indicators.note: one thing about another goes round it

parts.note: amorous means full of romantic passion
PH is the map abbreviation for public house

explanation.surface: Someone keen on the pub wonders whether things get hazy after a few drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: PH marks a pub on British Ordnance Survey maps; it goes inside the word for passionate.
explanation.definitionFit: Amorphous means lacking clear shape or form, so something vague and indistinct in outline.

clue.text: Base to conduct a search in naval battles

definitions.note: plural, while the answer is a singular mass noun covering many battles

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a seat is a base, as in the seat of power
to comb an area is to search it thoroughly
taken as written

explanation.surface: A naval base is used for running search operations during sea battles.
explanation.walkthrough: The search and the article go inside the base in the order COMB then A, a loose reading of 'a search'.
explanation.definitionFit: Combat at sea is fighting between warships, which is what naval battles consist of.

clue.text: Horse held in lovely position

indicators.note: something held in another is gripped inside it

parts.note: nice is a mild synonym for lovely
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: A horse is kept in a pleasant spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Horse is slang for heroin, whose drug abbreviation is H.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a comfortable or suitable role or place in life, a fitting spot for someone.

clue.text: Auditor having cosy pad near cape shows sincerity

parts.note: an auditor is a listener, and the ear does the listening
a nest is a snug home
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbour names

explanation.surface: An accountant with a snug flat on the coast proves to be honest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' suggests an accountant; it is literally a hearer. A ness is a promontory, common in British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnestness is seriousness of intent and genuine feeling, a close synonym for sincerity.

clue.text: One in 200 finding remedy?

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a hundred is a ton, and C is a hundred in Roman numerals
I is one in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: One person in two hundred finds a cure.
explanation.walkthrough: 200 is split as two hundreds written different ways: TON, the slang hundred, and C, the Roman one.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonic is a medicine or pick-me-up that restores health, so a remedy.

clue.text: Pitch in Fritzenbühel playable for a period

indicators.note: the answer appears only for a short stretch of the text, then ends

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A sports ground in an Alpine village is fit to play on for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' looks like a playing field; 'pitch in' is the definition. The Austrian-sounding name is there only to carry the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To pitch in is an idiom for joining a shared effort, so to assist or lend a hand.

clue.text: Raised drink holding one container

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters lifts them upwards, so they read backwards
what holds something has it inside

parts.note: to lap is to drink with the tongue, like a cat
I is one in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone lifts a glass that holds a single vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised drink' sounds like a toast; the drink is a verb, lapping, written upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A pail is a bucket, an open vessel for carrying water or other liquid.

clue.text: Leading lady twice dressing a son in rubber

indicators.note: dressing someone wraps clothes around them, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: ER is the Queen, written two times
A as written plus S for son

explanation.surface: A star actress twice dresses a boy in a rubber outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading lady' suggests a film star; it is the Queen, ER, the top woman of the land. Rubber is the British word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a rubber is the small block used to rub out pencil marks, which Americans call an eraser.

clue.text: Eve signs letter whose contents form short essay

indicators.note: the contents of something are what lies inside, so the outer letters are dropped

parts.note: the inside of this name
the inside of this word
the inside of this word

explanation.surface: Eve puts her name to a letter whose content makes a brief piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whose contents' looks as if it refers only to the letter, but it applies to all three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A vignette is a brief evocative description or sketch in prose, a short literary piece.

clue.text: Ram's insides in dish for taste

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a plate is a dish

indicators.note: insides are what lies within, so only the inner letter is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of this animal

explanation.surface: Offal from a ram is served in a dish to suit someone's taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ram's insides' suggests offal on a plate; it means the one middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Palate means a person's sense of flavour or discernment in food and drink.

clue.text: Naughty child accepting need for plague carrier?

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a brat is a badly behaved child
a lack is a need or want

explanation.surface: A badly behaved child who demands things is a real pest.
explanation.walkthrough: A naughty child can be called a plague, which suits the surface; the question mark flags that the carrier is the rodent, famed for spreading the Black Death through its fleas.
explanation.definitionFit: The black rat's fleas spread bubonic plague in medieval Europe, so it is the classic disease vector.
